## The Architecture of Cold in Capileira

At an altitude of 1,436 meters, Capileira is not content to be merely the highest village in the Barranco de Poqueira: it is also an architectural laboratory where the cold has dictated every construction decision for centuries. The 800 millimeters of annual precipitation and the average of twenty snowy days recorded by the AEMET station in the municipality forced master masons to develop solutions that today amaze with their relentless logic. The terrao, that flat roof made of launa waterproofed with lime, is not an aesthetic whim but a calculated response to the weight of snow. Unlike pitched roofs that collapse under extreme accumulations, the flat roof distributes the load evenly and allows the white blanket to act as a natural insulator during the harshest weeks of winter.

The truncated conical chimneys that crown the houses of Capileira tell the same story from another perspective. Their truncated cone shape, topped with a flat stone that acts as a hat, prevents snow from accumulating at the smoke outlet and blocking the draft. The design, passed down from generation to generation without blueprints or treatises, also solves a thermal problem: by narrowing towards the top, the chimney accelerates the exit of hot smoke and prevents cold air from descending into the hearth. The oldest residents recall that before the arrival of diesel and electricity, the wood-burning stove with its conical chimney was the thermal heart of the home, the only space where the temperature exceeded fifteen degrees on January nights.

The historical records of the Capileira meteorological station, part of the State Meteorological Agency, confirm minimum temperatures of twelve degrees below zero, making the village one of the coldest inhabited places in the province of Granada. Read in the abstract, that figure seems like just another piece of technical data; but applied to daily life, it explains the orientation of the facades, the thickness of the masonry walls, and the scarcity of windows on the north faces. Traditional houses open to the south and east, seeking the morning sun and sheltering from the westerly wind that sweeps down the slope. The walls, sixty centimeters thick in many cases, function as thermal accumulators that absorb daytime heat and release it slowly during the night.

The study 'Arquitectura alpujarreña y clima', conducted by researchers at the Universidad de Granada, documents how this construction model achieved a remarkable balance with the weather conditions of the high Mediterranean mountains. The authors of the work analyzed dozens of homes in Capileira, Bubión, and Pampaneira, measuring indoor and outdoor temperatures over a full year. Their conclusions indicate that the traditional Alpujarra house maintains an indoor thermal oscillation of just six degrees between day and night, compared to the twenty or twenty-five degrees of oscillation recorded outside. This stability, achieved without active climate control systems, represents a lesson in energy efficiency that contemporary architects are beginning to study closely.

The cold has not only shaped the buildings: it has also dictated the calendar of work and celebrations. The pig slaughter, which in the lower villages of the Alpujarra takes place in December, is brought forward to November in Capileira to take advantage of the first hard frosts that guarantee the preservation of the meat. The steep streets, designed to quickly drain rainwater, become channels of melting snow during the thaws of February and March. Residents place flat stones at their door thresholds to prevent water from entering the homes when the white blanket begins to melt. Every detail of the public space responds to a specific climatic need, even if the occasional visitor only perceives the picturesque charm of the whitewashed facades.

However, the data handled by the inhabitants of Capileira themselves paint a picture of accelerated transformation. The residents consulted confirm that the snow lasts less than it did four decades ago: from the sixty days of continuous cover recorded in 1980, it has dropped to twenty-five in 2024. This figure, corroborated by the historical series of AEMET and by the observations of the shepherds who go up to the puerto de la Carihuela, implies that the snow cycle that for centuries regulated the architecture, agriculture, and social life of the village is drastically shortening. The elders remember winters when the snow covered the terraos for two months straight, forcing them to shovel paths from the houses to the public fountain.

This reduction in the snow period has direct consequences for the maintenance of traditional homes. The terrao, designed to bear the weight of a snow cover that no longer arrives with the same intensity, now requires different maintenance: the launa cracks more easily without the constant moisture that used to compact it, and water leaks multiply during months of heavy rain. Local masons, heirs to a craft passed down from father to son, have had to adapt traditional techniques to a climate that no longer behaves as it once did. Some owners opt for synthetic waterproofing that alters the original aesthetic; others stick with lime and launa, accepting that annual maintenance will be more costly.

The paradox of Capileira lies in the fact that its architecture, born of extreme cold, has become a tourist attraction precisely when the cold is beginning to recede. Visitors who wander its streets in search of the perfect Alpujarra postcard—white terraos, conical chimneys, snow-capped mountains in the background—rarely perceive that they are looking at a climatic adaptation in the process of falling out of sync. The study by the Universidad de Granada warns that the loss of climatic functionality of traditional architecture could accelerate its abandonment or its transformation into second homes with conventional heating systems. The result would be a paradox difficult to resolve: the village that best knew how to adapt to the cold of the high mountains could end up losing the very architecture that made it possible.
